segments.title: (whole paper)
segments.reason: The paper's central assertion (abstract + Theorem 1.1) is: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex v with |N+_1(v)| ≤ |N+_2(v)|. The Lean captures this exactly. `IsOriented` requires `loopless` (no loops) and `asymmetric` (r u v → ¬ r v u, i.e. no pair of opposite arcs); representing the graph as a Prop relation r : V→V→Prop forbids multiple arcs — matching the paper's definition of an oriented graph, with no added connectivity/completeness assumption. `firstNeighbors r v = {w : r v w}` is N+_1(v); `secondNeighbors r v = {w : w ≠ v ∧ ¬ r v w ∧ ∃ u, r v u ∧ r u w}` is exactly N+_2(v) (distance exactly two, excluding v and the first out-neighborhood, counted once). `GoodVertex r v := (firstNeighbors r v).card ≤ (secondNeighbors r v).card` is |N+_1(v)| ≤ |N+_2(v)|. The main result `exists_goodVertex (r) (hr : IsOriented r) : ∃ v, GoodVertex r v` under `[Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]` (nonempty finite) is precisely Theorem 1.1, same quantifiers and inequality direction. The whole proof pipeline described in the strategy (minimal counterexample reduction → strict subset inequality → transitive-tournament blowup → pruning lemma for finite binary relations → extremal contradiction) is present and structurally mirrors the sections, and the sink/positive-indegree facts align. The only paper claims not formalized are the §5 weighted forms (Cor. 5.1) and §6 directed-cycle consequences (Cor. 6.1), but these are explicitly downstream consequences obtained via Seacrest's pre-existing external equivalences, not the theorem under formalization; the headline theorem itself is faithfully and completely captured.
